The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) regulates workplace health and safety in Great Britain
(England, Scotland and Wales). This notebook uses two of its sources:

- **RIDDOR**: injuries that employers must report under the *Reporting of Injuries, Diseases and
  Dangerous Occurrences Regulations*: deaths, "specified" injuries (such as fractures and
  amputations), and injuries that keep an employee off work for more than 7 days.
- **The Labour Force Survey (LFS)**: a household survey in which workers report whether they
  were injured at work in the last 12 months.

Comparing them shows how much employers under-report. Read the module [README](../README.md)
and [data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.

# Part 0. Load the data

The tables in `data/tidy/` are complete for the breakdowns they cover and are committed to the
repository. HSE years run from April to March: "2024/25" is 1 April 2024 to 31 March 2025, and
`year` is the year it ends (2025).

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)

tidy_dir <- "../data/tidy"
github <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/",
                 "main/modules/uk-hse-riddor/data/tidy")
read_tidy <- function(name) {
  local <- file.path(tidy_dir, name)
  read_csv(if (file.exists(local)) local else file.path(github, name),
           col_types = cols(.default = col_character())) |>
    mutate(across(any_of("year"), as.integer),
           across(any_of(c("value", "estimate", "ci_lower", "ci_upper")), as.numeric),
           across(any_of("low_sample"), as.logical))
}

history <- read_tidy("riddor_history.csv")           # since 1974, broad industries
industry <- read_tidy("riddor_industry.csv.gz")      # detailed industry, 2014/15 onward
kind <- read_tidy("riddor_kind.csv.gz")              # kind of accident
age_gender <- read_tidy("riddor_age_gender.csv.gz")
nature_site <- read_tidy("riddor_nature_site.csv")
fatal <- read_tidy("riddor_fatal_latest.csv")        # deaths, 2021/22 to 2025/26
lfs <- read_tidy("lfs_injury.csv.gz")                # self-reported injuries (survey)

# Shorter industry names for plots, for example "Construction (SIC F)" -> "Construction"
short_industry <- function(x) str_trunc(str_remove(x, " \\(SIC.*\\)$"), 45)
```

# Part 1. Fifty years of work-related deaths

```{r fatal-trend}
fatal_trend <- history |>
  filter(industry == "All industries", injury_type == "Fatal",
         worker_group %in% c("Workers", "Members of the public"), measure == "count",
         year >= 1981)

ggplot(fatal_trend, aes(year, value, colour = worker_group)) +
  geom_line() +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(title = "Work-related deaths reported under RIDDOR, Great Britain",
       x = "Year ending", y = "Deaths", colour = NULL)

history |>
  filter(industry == "All industries", injury_type == "Fatal", worker_group == "Workers",
         measure == "rate_per_100000", year %in% c(1982, 1992, 2002, 2012, 2022, 2025)) |>
  select(period, deaths_per_100000_workers = value)
```

# Part 2. Which industries are most dangerous?

The latest file gives a five-year total (2021/22 to 2025/26), which is more stable than any one year.

```{r industries}
fatal_by_industry <- fatal |>
  filter(breakdown == "industry", period_length == "5-year total", worker_group == "Workers",
         !str_starts(category, "- of which"), !category %in% c("All industries (SIC A-U)", "Missing Industry")) |>
  select(category, measure, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = value) |>
  rename(deaths = count, rate = rate_per_100000) |>
  mutate(industry = short_industry(category)) |>
  arrange(desc(rate))
select(fatal_by_industry, industry, deaths, rate)

ggplot(fatal_by_industry, aes(rate, fct_reorder(industry, rate))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Fatal injury rate by industry, 2021/22 to 2025/26",
       x = "Deaths per 100,000 workers per year", y = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. Which industry has by far the highest rate? Which has the most deaths?
2. Agriculture's rate is many times the average. Name two features of farm work (think about
   who does it and where) that might explain this.

**Your answer:**



# Part 3. How do workers die, and how are they injured?

```{r kinds}
deaths_by_kind <- fatal |>
  filter(breakdown == "kind of accident", period_length == "5-year total",
         worker_group == "Workers", category != "All accident kinds") |>
  transmute(accident_kind = category, deaths = value)

injuries_by_kind <- kind |>
  filter(sic_section == "A-U", year == max(year), injury_type == "All non-fatal",
         measure == "count", accident_kind != "All accident kinds") |>
  transmute(accident_kind, non_fatal_injuries = value)

full_join(deaths_by_kind, injuries_by_kind, by = c("accident_kind")) |>
  mutate(share_of_deaths = deaths / sum(deaths),
         share_of_injuries = non_fatal_injuries / sum(non_fatal_injuries)) |>
  arrange(desc(deaths))
```

**Questions**

1. What are the three most common kinds of fatal accident? The three most common kinds of
   non-fatal injury?
2. Slips and trips cause many injuries but few deaths. Falls from height are the reverse. Why?
3. Acts of violence cause many non-fatal injuries. In which industries would you expect these?

**Your answer:**



# Part 4. How many injuries are not reported?

RIDDOR counts the injuries employers report. The LFS asks workers directly. Both have a measure
of injuries keeping someone off work for **more than 7 days** (RIDDOR counts employees only).

```{r under-reporting}
riddor_over7 <- history |>
  filter(industry == "All industries", worker_group == "Employees", injury_type == "Over-7-day",
         measure == "count") |>
  transmute(year, source = "RIDDOR (reported by employers)", injuries = value)

lfs_over7 <- lfs |>
  filter(breakdown == "all", injury_type == "Over-7-day absence", measure == "injuries_thousands") |>
  transmute(year, source = "LFS (reported by workers)", injuries = estimate * 1000,
            lower = ci_lower * 1000, upper = ci_upper * 1000)

bind_rows(riddor_over7, lfs_over7) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, injuries, colour = source)) +
  geom_ribbon(data = lfs_over7, aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper, fill = source), alpha = 0.2,
              colour = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(title = "Injuries with more than 7 days off work", x = "Year ending",
       y = "Injuries per year", colour = NULL, fill = NULL)

lfs |>
  filter(breakdown == "all", measure == "injuries_thousands", year == max(year)) |>
  select(injury_type, estimate, ci_lower, ci_upper)
```

**Questions**

1. In the latest year, about how many over-7-day injuries did workers report in the LFS, and how
   many did employers report under RIDDOR? Roughly what fraction were reported?
2. The LFS estimate includes the self-employed and the RIDDOR count does not. Does that make the
   gap bigger or smaller than it looks?
3. Give three reasons an employer might not report an injury.
4. HSE calls the LFS its preferred source for the *number* of non-fatal injuries. What can RIDDOR
   tell you that a survey cannot?

**Your answer:**



# Part 5. Age and gender

```{r age-gender}
age_gender |>
  filter(sic_section == "A-U", age_group == "All", injury_type == "Fatal",
         worker_group == "Workers", measure == "count") |>
  group_by(gender) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(value))

age_gender |>
  # Fatal rates are per 100,000 workers; non-fatal rates per 100,000 employees
  filter(sic_section == "A-U", gender == "All", measure == "rate_per_100000",
         (injury_type == "Fatal" & worker_group == "Workers") |
           (injury_type == "All non-fatal" & worker_group == "Employees"),
         !age_group %in% c("All", "Unknown", "Under 16")) |>
  group_by(injury_type, age_group) |>
  summarise(mean_rate = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = injury_type, values_from = mean_rate)
```

**Questions**

1. What share of deaths are men? Why?
2. How do fatal and non-fatal injury rates change with age? The fatal rate rises much more
   steeply. Give two reasons why an injury is more likely to be fatal for an older worker.

# Part 6. Under-reporting by industry

The LFS is a survey, so its estimates have **95% confidence intervals**. Here we compare the LFS
rate of over-7-day injuries with the RIDDOR rate for each industry section over the latest
five years.

```{r reporting-ratio, fig.height = 7}
lfs_sections <- lfs |>
  filter(breakdown == "industry", level == "Section", period_length == "5 year",
         injury_type == "Over-7-day absence", measure == "rate_per_100000_workers",
         year == max(year)) |>
  select(sic = code, industry = category, period, lfs_rate = estimate, ci_lower, ci_upper) |>
  filter(!is.na(lfs_rate))   # sections with too few survey respondents have no estimate
lfs_sections

riddor_sections <- industry |>
  filter(sic_level == "Section", worker_group == "Employees", injury_type == "Over-7-day",
         measure == "rate_per_100000", year > max(year) - 5) |>
  mutate(sic = str_extract(sic_code, "^[A-Z]")) |>
  group_by(sic) |>
  summarise(riddor_rate = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE))

comparison <- lfs_sections |>
  inner_join(riddor_sections, by = "sic") |>
  mutate(reported_share = riddor_rate / lfs_rate) |>
  arrange(reported_share)
select(comparison, industry, lfs_rate, riddor_rate, reported_share)

ggplot(comparison, aes(lfs_rate, fct_reorder(str_trunc(industry, 40), lfs_rate))) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = ci_lower, xmax = ci_upper)) +
  geom_point(aes(x = riddor_rate), colour = "red") +
  labs(title = "Over-7-day injury rates: LFS (black, with 95% CI) and RIDDOR (red)",
       x = "Injuries per 100,000 workers per year", y = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. In which industries is the reported share lowest? Highest? Suggest reasons.
2. The LFS rate is per worker and the RIDDOR rate is per employee, and the LFS counts consecutive
   calendar days off. How might these differences bias the reported share?
3. Some industries have wide confidence intervals. Why, and what does that mean for comparing them?

**Your answer:**



# Part 7. Breaks in a time series

Reporting rules changed several times. Each change affects what counts as a "reportable" injury.

```{r breaks}
changes <- tibble(year = c(1986, 1996, 2012, 2013),
                  change = c("RIDDOR 1985: over-3-day injuries reportable",
                             "RIDDOR 1995: wider list of major injuries",
                             "Threshold raised to over-7-day",
                             "RIDDOR 2013: 'specified' injuries"))

history |>
  filter(industry == "All industries", worker_group == "Employees", injury_type != "Fatal",
         measure == "count") |>
  ggplot(aes(year, value, colour = injury_type)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(data = changes, aes(xintercept = year + 1), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Non-fatal injuries to employees reported under RIDDOR and earlier regulations",
       x = "Year ending", y = "Reported injuries", colour = NULL)

changes
```

**Questions**

1. For each dashed line, describe what happened to the series and whether the change reflects
   safety or reporting rules.
2. Between rule changes, reported injuries fell steadily. How could you tell whether that is a
   real fall in injuries? (Hint: compare with the LFS in Part 4.)
3. What happened in 2020/21?

**Your answer:**



# Part 8. Comparing countries

The fatal injury rate in Great Britain is about 0.4 deaths per 100,000 workers. In the US
(CFOI module) it is about 3.3 to 3.5, and in Australia (Safe Work Australia module) about 1.5.
